newsitem.title: USA: Clinton proposing ways to bring races together.
newsitem.headline: Clinton proposing ways to bring races together.

text.p: President Bill Clinton steps into the simmering cauldron of race in the United States on Saturday with a major speech encouraging a racially diverse, often combative population to come together as "one America."

A son of the South who witnessed the civil rights upheavals of the 1960s, Clinton is using his commencement address at the University of California at San Diego to launch a year-long look at the race issue.

"If there is any issue I ought to have credibility on, it is this one, because it is a part of who I am and what I've done," said Clinton, who as an 11-year-old watched the forced integration of Little Rock Central High School in his home state of Arkansas.

With Clinton were the seven members of an advisory board he appointed on Thursday to conduct town hall meetings, examine the state of race relations in the country and in a year give Americans a report outlining "facts, not myths" about the problems and ways to solve them.
"I think that there are problems," Clinton said on Friday. "I think things are better than they used to be, but I think that we have a lot of work to do in order to be one America."
The initiative comes at a time when African-Americans feel they are being left behind in the country's economic good times, their communities ravaged by bloodshed, crime and drugs.

At the same time some whites feel government policies giving minorities preferences on hiring and education are edging them out. To the distress of minorities, these so-called affirmative action programmes are increasingly under fire. The state of California eliminated them, a decision the Clinton administration is fighting in court.

A Gallup Poll this week found persistent gaps in attitudes and perceptions between blacks and whites. For example it said whites characterise themselves as having very little personal prejudice against blacks, but that blacks feel whites have higher levels of racial prejudice than whites believe about themselves.

There is no doubt that racism remains a pervasive force in many parts of America. The Ku Klux Klan still burns crosses in the South. Even John Hope Franklin, 82-year-old chairman of the new advisory panel, said recently that, "We have a slave mentality working in this country. I am still called 'boy' sometimes."
Clinton sees now as the time to address the issue because of projections that by the year 2050, the minority population will rise to total 47 percent and the white majority decline to 53 percent.
"If you look at where we are and where we're going, we will soon be, in the next few decades a multiracial group in which no racial group is in a majority," he said.

There has been no major incident to create a backdrop for Clinton's action, like the 1992 riots in Los Angeles, but as one White House aide put it: "Race is clearly one of those things that America has been sweeping under the rug for a long time, and the rug is starting to bulge."
Civil rights leaders who have been sceptical of the president's commitment to improving the lives of black Americans were waiting to hear what specific proposals Clinton will have in his remarks.

The Rev. Jesse Jackson, who was a follower of slain civil rights leader Martin Luther King, believes Clinton should set an example by hiring more minorities in the federal government, particularly the White House, appoint more minorities as federal judges and improve enforcement of anti-discrimination laws.
Clinton would like to make bridging the racial gap a lasting legacy of his presidency, to succeed where others have failed.

"We undertake this initiative knowing that, at the end of the day, it may not work and we might not be able to change attitudes about race in America," said White House spokesman Mike McCurry. "That doesn't make it any less important to make the effort."
